notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 2 Kings 14, drawn from the sources I was able to reach. Where I could not find material, I note that.

---

## Verses 1–4: Amaziah's Accession and Summary of His Reign

**v. 1:** Amaziah ("Yahweh is mighty") became king in the second year of Jehoash (also called Joash) of Israel. Gill notes a chronological puzzle: since Joash of Israel began reigning in the 37th year of Joash of Judah (who reigned 40 years), Amaziah should have begun in Joash of Israel's *fourth* year. Gill resolves this by suggesting the "second year" counts from when Joash of Israel reigned alone, after a 2–3 year co-regency with his father.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

Dr. Constable dates Amaziah's reign to 796–767 BC.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html

**v. 2:** Amaziah was 25 at his accession and reigned 29 years. His mother Jehoaddan was from Jerusalem. Grant's Commentary suggests she "must have been a commendable character, for her son was comparatively obedient to the Lord."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/2-kings-14.html

**v. 3:** He "did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, yet not like David his father." Precept Austin explains: "David is the gold standard for Judah's kings … a man who was not sinless, but who was wholeheartedly devoted to Yahweh, was responsive to rebuke and willing to repent, and did not tolerate rival worship." Amaziah's obedience "fell short of the Davidic ideal." The parallel in 2 Chronicles 25:2 adds the diagnosis: "yet not with a whole heart." G. Campbell Morgan (quoted at Precept Austin) says the "imperfection of heart consists in incomplete surrender. Some chamber of the temple is closed against the true Indweller."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-14-commentary

Matthew Henry adds: "It is not enough to do that which our pious predecessors did, merely to keep up the usage, but we must do it as they did it, from the same principle of faith and devotion and with the same sincerity and resolution."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

David Guzik notes: "Compared to Joash, Amaziah faithfully continued his policies. Yet some of those policies allowed compromises… Compared to David … Amaziah did not match up favorably."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

Gill says he did right "at least externally, and at the beginning of his reign."
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 4:** The high places were not removed; the people continued sacrificing there. This refrain recurs throughout Kings. Matthew Henry: "It is hard to get clear of those corruptions which, by long usage, have gained both prescription and a favourable opinion." Precept Austin notes that high-place worship violated Deuteronomy 12:13–14, which required sacrifices only at the place God chose.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-14-commentary
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

---

## Verses 5–6: Justice on His Father's Murderers

**v. 5:** Once his hold on the kingdom was secure, Amaziah executed the servants who had assassinated his father Joash. Matthew Henry commends his prudence in waiting "lest it should occasion some disturbance … Justice strikes surely by striking slowly." Gill notes Amaziah waited until "the idolatry and murder his father had committed were worn off of the minds of the people."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 6:** Amaziah did *not* execute the children of the murderers, explicitly obeying Deuteronomy 24:16: "Fathers must not be put to death for their children." Guzik calls this "an act of faith that defied the standards of his own time" — the ancient Near Eastern practice was to execute the whole family of a regicide. Constable agrees: "Amaziah instead trusted God to control the potential rebels." Poole (quoted by Guzik) says: "Wherein he showed some faith and courage, that he would obey this command of God, though it was very hazardous to himself, such persons being likely to seek revenge for their father's death."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html

Matthew Henry notes that advisers probably urged him to kill the children "both in revenge … and in policy, that the children might not plot against him." Amaziah instead trusted God with the outcome.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

---

## Verse 7: Victory over Edom

**v. 7:** Amaziah struck down 10,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt (south of the Dead Sea) and captured Sela, renaming it Joktheel. Gill identifies Sela (meaning "rock") with Petra, the capital of Edom. He notes Joktheel means "the obedience of God," given "in memory of his obedience to the prophet of the Lord, in consequence of which he obtained this victory."
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

Guzik fills in the background from 2 Chronicles 25:5–16: Amaziah assembled 300,000 Judean troops and hired 100,000 Israelite mercenaries. A prophet told him to dismiss the Israelites; he obeyed, trusting God despite the financial loss, and God gave victory. But immediately afterward, Amaziah brought back Edomite gods and worshipped them (2 Chr. 25:14) — his heart turned from God right after the triumph.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

Dr. Constable notes that Edom had revolted from Judah during Jehoram's reign, and Amaziah was subduing them again.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html

---

## Verses 8–12: The Foolish Challenge to Jehoash of Israel

**v. 8:** Elated by victory, Amaziah sent messengers challenging Jehoash of Israel: "Come, let us meet face to face" (i.e., in battle). Guzik explains the political background: the dismissed Israelite mercenaries, angry at missing plunder, had raided Judean towns on their way home, killing 3,000 (2 Chr. 25:13). Amaziah also may have hoped to reunite the kingdoms under Judah by force. Matthew Henry calls him "proud, presumptuous, and prodigal of blood."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

**vv. 9–10:** Jehoash replied with a parable: "A thistle in Lebanon sent to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son in marriage.' Then a wild beast … trampled the thistle." Guzik explains: the thistle is Amaziah (lowly, prickly, weak), the cedar is Jehoash (tall, established). The wild beast trampling the thistle shows how easily Israel could crush Judah. He then warned plainly: "Your heart has become proud. Glory in that and stay at home."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

Gill notes the proverb's point: Jehoash would have scorned even a peaceful marriage alliance with Amaziah, let alone a military challenge.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

Matthew Henry: "See where the root of all sin lies; it is in the heart … It is not Providence, the event, the occasion (whatever it is), that makes men proud … but it is their own heart that does it."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 11:** Amaziah refused to listen. The two kings met at Beth-shemesh in Judah. Gill says this was a judicial hardening: "for this was of God, and by his overruling providence, that he might be punished for his idolatry, in setting up the gods of Edom" (citing 2 Chr. 25:14, 20).
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 12:** "Judah was routed before Israel, and every man fled to his home." Josephus (cited by both Gill and Matthew Henry) says a sudden terror seized Judah's army and they fled before joining battle.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

---

## Verses 13–14: The Consequences of Defeat

**v. 13:** Jehoash captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, marched to Jerusalem, and broke down 400 cubits (about 600 feet / 180 metres) of the city wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. Gill and Josephus say Jehoash drove his chariot through the breach in triumph.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

Guzik stresses the theological cause: "Amaziah had a mighty army and Jehoash had a weak army. Yet God gave Israel the victory over Judah to rebuke the idolatry of Amaziah. It came from God, that He might give them into the hand of their enemies, because they sought the gods of Edom" (2 Chr. 25:20).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

**v. 14:** Jehoash plundered "all the gold and silver and all the articles found in the house of the LORD" and the royal treasuries, took hostages, and returned to Samaria. Guzik notes that Amaziah's foolish decision hurt the whole kingdom: "It wasn't just a loss of his personal wealth … but also of the gold and silver of God's people." The hostages likely included sons of Judean princes, taken as security (Gill, citing the Targum).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

---

## Verses 15–16: Death of Jehoash of Israel

**vv. 15–16:** A closing summary for Jehoash (Joash) of Israel: his acts are recorded in the chronicles of the kings of Israel; he was buried in Samaria; his son Jeroboam (II) succeeded him. This repeats the formula from 2 Kings 13:12–13. Matthew Henry notes the repetition occurs because "the historian had occasion to give a further account of his life and actions."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

---

## Verses 17–20: Amaziah's Decline and Assassination

**v. 17:** Amaziah lived 15 years after Jehoash died. Some commentators infer that Amaziah was released from captivity in Israel upon Jehoash's death. Guzik quotes Trapp: "But it was a kind of a lifeless life … He lay all the while under the hatred and contempt of his subjects."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

**v. 18:** The standard formula referring to the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah. Matthew Henry pointedly notes: "His acts are said to be found written … but not his might; for his cruelty when he was a conqueror over the Edomites, and his insolence when he challenged the king of Israel, showed him void of true courage."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 19:** A conspiracy formed against him in Jerusalem. Amaziah fled to Lachish (a fortified city in southwestern Judah), but assassins pursued and killed him there. Constable says the conspirators "were evidently Judahites who wanted to restore pure worship to their nation (2 Chr. 25:27)." Gill suggests the conspirators may have been those whose sons were taken as hostages by Jehoash, blaming Amaziah for the disaster.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

Guzik notes the irony: Amaziah was assassinated just like his father Joash was (2 Kings 12:20–21). Knapp (quoted by Guzik) adds: "Lachish was the first of the cities of Judah to adopt the idolatries of the kingdom of Israel … and it was natural for the idolatrous Amaziah to seek an asylum there."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

Dilday (quoted by Guzik) raises the possibility "the assassins … may have been the very children whom Amaziah had spared. They, in turn, were exacting vengeance for Amaziah's executions."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

**v. 20:** Amaziah was brought back on horses and buried in Jerusalem with his fathers. Gill notes a Jewish tradition that because he worshipped Edomite gods (which were carried on horses), he was carried on horses rather than on the shoulders of men.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

---

## Verses 21–22: Azariah (Uzziah) Succeeds Amaziah

**v. 21:** "All the people of Judah took Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king." Azariah is also called Uzziah ("help of the Lord" / "strength of the Lord"). Gill notes a chronological difficulty: if Azariah was 16 at his accession and Jeroboam II began in Amaziah's 15th year (v. 23), the numbers seem to conflict — but this is resolved by positing a co-regency. Constable notes that Azariah likely began as co-regent when Amaziah was taken prisoner (c. 790 BC). Matthew Henry suggests a 12-year interregnum with protectors governing until Azariah came of age.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 22:** Azariah rebuilt Elath (an Edomite port on the Gulf of Aqaba) and restored it to Judah. Constable suggests Amaziah's earlier defeat of Edom made this possible.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html

---

## Verses 23–29: Jeroboam II of Israel

**v. 23:** Jeroboam II began his reign in Samaria in Amaziah's 15th year and reigned 41 years — the longest reign in the Northern Kingdom's history. Constable dates it 793–753 BC, with the first 12 years as co-regent with his father Jehoash.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html

**v. 24:** "He did evil in the sight of the LORD and did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit" — i.e., the golden calf worship at Dan and Bethel. Matthew Henry observes the irony that the house of Jehu, which had destroyed Baal worship, clung to the calf cult: "But a sin is never the less evil in God's sight, whatever it is in ours, for its being an ancient usage."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 25:** Despite his wickedness, Jeroboam II restored Israel's territory from Lebo-hamath (in the north) to the Sea of the Arabah (the Dead Sea, in the south). This fulfilled a prophecy spoken through "Jonah son of Amittai" — the same Jonah who was later sent to Nineveh. Guzik notes: "Apparently he also had a ministry among his own people, not only among the people of Nineveh." Gill says this is "the first of the prophets spoken of whose books are extant," and notes his hometown Gath-hepher was in Zebulun (Galilee), contradicting the later claim that "no prophet comes out of Galilee" (John 7:52).
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 26:** The reason for God's mercy: "The LORD saw that the affliction of the Israelites, both slave and free, was very bitter. There was no one to help Israel." Constable explains: "This probably means that everyone in Israel was suffering before Jeroboam II began to improve conditions." The phrase "none shut up or left" means total devastation — no one escaped the affliction. God acted purely out of compassion, not because Israel repented. Matthew Henry: "Though he saw not any signs of their repentance … yet he saw their affliction."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_kings/14.htm

**v. 27:** The Lord "had said that He would not blot out the name of Israel from under heaven." Gill says this means God "had not as yet declared it by any of his prophets," though He later would through Hosea (Hosea 1:4–9), fulfilled in the reign of Hoshea (2 Kings 17). So "He saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Jehoash." Morgan comments: "It seems to suggest amazement in his mind as he contemplated the patience of Jehovah with the sinning nation."
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

Guzik: "Out of great mercy, God showed kindness to a disobedient Israel ruled by an evil king." Constable adds: "Times of material prosperity have usually proved to be more difficult for God's people to handle successfully than times of adversity."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html

**v. 28:** Jeroboam II's military exploits — recovering Damascus and Hamath — are referred to the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. Gill notes a debate: did Jeroboam recover these for Israel, or (per Kimchi) did he recover them and restore them to Judah, to whom they had belonged since David and Solomon? Guzik adds that God used the rising Assyrian Empire to weaken Syria, which enabled Israel's expansion under Jeroboam II.
— https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/14.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

Guzik notes archaeological evidence: "In the age prior to Jeroboam II, the houses in Israel's cities were roughly the same size. But archaeologists find a change starting in the eighth century b.c. — ancient cities like Tirzah have a neighborhood of large, expensive houses and another neighborhood of small, crowded structures." This matches the denunciations in Amos 2:6–7, 8:4–6.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

**v. 29:** Jeroboam II "rested with his fathers" and his son Zechariah succeeded him. This was the fourth generation of Jehu's dynasty, fulfilling the promise in 2 Kings 10:30. Guzik quotes Knapp: "From the time of Jeroboam's death, declension set in, ending less than seventy years later in its final overthrow and dissolution."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-14/

## Tradition-Specific Readings

**Reformed / Puritan (Matthew Henry, Gill):** Both stress God's sovereignty behind the events. Amaziah's defeat is divine chastisement for idolatry; Jeroboam II's prosperity is undeserved mercy. Matthew Henry underlines that outward prosperity does not indicate God's approval of a ruler. Gill emphasizes the judicial hardening of Amaziah — God gave him over to pride for his destruction.

**Dispensational / Dallas Seminary (Constable):** Constable gives careful attention to chronology (co-regencies, dates to the exact year) and archaeology. He dates Amaziah to 796–767 BC and Jeroboam II to 793–753 BC with a 12-year co-regency. He also identifies the prophet Joel as possibly ministering in Judah during Amaziah's reign.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-kings-14.html

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word):** Guzik reads the narrative with a strong applicational thrust: military success and material prosperity, even God-given, can trap believers in pride. He stresses that leaders' foolish decisions harm their whole community. He also highlights archaeological confirmation and the prophets Amos and Hosea as contemporary witnesses.

**Methodist / Holiness (Pulpit Commentary Homiletics):** The Pulpit Homiletics section draws broader theological lessons — God's respect for human freedom (allowing wicked kings to rule), the self-punishing nature of sin ("Sin is suicidal"), and the necessity of faith in a future rectification: "Who could love a Supreme Existence, which could permit forever such a state of existence as we have here? There must come a day of rectification."
— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/2_kings/14.htm
